subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is meant by 'social stratification'?
options: The way society is divided into a hierarchy of unequal layers or groups
The movement of people from one country to another
The process of forming friendship groups at school
The division of a workforce into separate shifts
questions.explain: Social stratification refers to the arrangement of society into ranked layers or strata that are unequal in wealth, status and power.

questions.q: A status that a person is given at birth and cannot easily change is called what?
questions.explain: Ascribed status is fixed at birth, such as being born into a particular caste, unlike achieved status which is earned through effort.

questions.q: Which feature best describes the caste system as a type of stratification?
options: It is a closed system in which movement between strata is not allowed
It is an open system based mainly on personal achievement
It rewards individuals according to their qualifications
It allows people to rise through hard work and merit
questions.explain: The caste system is a closed system where position is ascribed at birth and social mobility between castes is effectively impossible.

questions.q: According to Karl Marx, society under capitalism is divided mainly into which two classes?
options: The upper class and the middle class
questions.explain: Marx argued capitalist society is split between the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, and the proletariat, who sell their labour.

questions.q: Functionalists such as Davis and Moore argue that social stratification is:
options: Necessary and beneficial because it ensures important roles are filled by able people
A form of exploitation that only benefits the ruling class
Something that will disappear under capitalism
Entirely based on inherited caste position
questions.explain: Davis and Moore claimed stratification is functional because unequal rewards motivate the most talented people to train for the most important positions.

questions.q: The movement of individuals up or down the social hierarchy is known as:
questions.explain: Social mobility describes the movement of individuals or groups between different positions in the stratification system.

questions.q: The idea that some working-class people are becoming more middle class in their attitudes and lifestyle is called:
questions.explain: Embourgeoisement is the theory that better-paid workers are adopting middle-class values and lifestyles.

questions.q: A society claims that anyone can succeed if they work hard, and rewards go to those with the most ability. This best reflects the idea of a:
questions.explain: A meritocracy allocates rewards and positions on the basis of individual merit, effort and ability rather than birth.

questions.q: What is the difference between wealth and income?
options: Wealth is the value of assets a person owns, while income is money received over a period of time
Wealth is money earned monthly, while income is property owned
Wealth and income mean exactly the same thing
Wealth is only cash savings, while income is only wages
questions.explain: Wealth refers to accumulated assets such as property, savings and shares, whereas income is the flow of money received, for example wages or benefits.

questions.q: Which statement best describes absolute poverty?
options: Lacking the basic necessities needed to survive, such as food, shelter and clean water
Being poorer than most other people in your society
Being unable to afford holidays and luxuries
Having a lower income than the national average
questions.explain: Absolute poverty is a lack of the minimum resources needed for physical survival, unlike relative poverty which is judged against the living standards of the wider society.

questions.q: A family is considered poor because they cannot afford the standard of living regarded as normal in their society. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Relative poverty measures deprivation in comparison with the normal living standards of the society in which a person lives.

questions.q: Which sociologist is associated with the idea of a 'culture of poverty'?
questions.explain: Oscar Lewis argued that the poor develop a distinctive culture of poverty, with values and attitudes passed on that help to keep them trapped in poverty.

questions.q: A person earns slightly more from a job than they received in benefits, but loses so much benefit that they are barely better off working. This situation is best described as the:
questions.explain: The poverty trap occurs when taking paid work leaves people little or no better off because of lost benefits and increased tax.

questions.q: The state provision of services such as benefits, healthcare and education to reduce poverty is known as the:
questions.explain: The welfare state is a system in which the government provides for the social and economic well-being of citizens, helping to relieve poverty.

questions.q: The invisible barrier that prevents many women from reaching the top positions in an organisation is called the:
questions.explain: The glass ceiling is an unofficial barrier of discrimination that blocks women (and some minority groups) from reaching senior positions.

questions.q: A social system in which men hold most of the power and dominate over women is known as:
questions.explain: Patriarchy refers to a society or system in which men hold the majority of power and authority over women.

questions.q: The tendency for women to make up a growing proportion of those living in poverty is called the:
questions.explain: The feminisation of poverty describes the trend of women being over-represented among the poor, linked to factors such as lower pay and lone parenthood.

questions.q: When discrimination against an ethnic group is built into the everyday practices and procedures of an organisation, this is best described as:
questions.explain: Institutional racism occurs when the normal working practices of an organisation systematically disadvantage members of ethnic minority groups.

questions.q: During an economic crisis, a minority ethnic group is unfairly blamed for rising unemployment. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Scapegoating is unfairly blaming a particular group, often a minority, for wider social or economic problems.

questions.q: According to Max Weber, authority based on established customs and long-standing tradition is called:
questions.explain: Weber identified traditional authority as legitimacy based on custom and long-established practices, such as the rule of a hereditary monarch.

questions.q: Weber used the term 'life chances' to refer to:
options: A person's opportunities to obtain the good things in life, such as good health, education and housing
The random luck a person has during their lifetime
The chance of a person changing their gender role
The likelihood of a society experiencing a revolution
questions.explain: For Weber, life chances are the opportunities individuals have to improve their quality of life, strongly shaped by their position in the stratification system.

questions.q: An elected government passes laws that citizens obey because they were made through official, accepted procedures. Weber would call this:
questions.explain: Rational-legal authority rests on a system of accepted rules and legal procedures, typical of modern states and bureaucracies.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Sociology (0495) syllabus; Social Inequality
